newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Croat pleads not guilty at U.N. war crimes court.
newsitem.headline: Croat pleads not guilty at U.N. war crimes court.

text.p: A Bosnian Croat pleaded not guilty on Tuesday at the U.N. War Crimes Tribunal in the Hague to atrocities committed against Moslems held at a prison camp he commanded during the Bosnian war.
Zlatko Aleksovski, 37, wearing a grey suit and dark tie, stood to enter his plea of not guilty of all charges at a preliminary hearing of Hague-based international court.
"I deny all culpability for these charges and do not feel responsible. Therefore I plead not guilty," he told French Judge Claude Jorda. "I consider myself absolutely innocent."
The court's indictment says Aleksovski was commander of the Kaonik prison camp in the Lasva Valley region of central Bosnia in early 1993, when the atrocities took place.
Detainees under his control were subjected to inhumane treatment, interrogation, used as human shields and some were murdered or otherwise killed, the tribunal says.
No date was set for the start of a trial, but the court agreed to meet on June 6 to begin moving the process forward.

Aleksovski was handed over to the Hague court on Monday, becoming the first war crimes suspect to be extradited by Croatia, after the West stepped up pressure on the country to cooperate with the U.N. body.

Last month the United States abstained from a vote by the International Monetary Fund to approve almost $500 million in loans to Croatia, as a sign of its dismay at Croatia's refusal to hand over suspects.
As the biggest and most influential donor to both the IMF and World Bank, U.S. lobbying could damage Croatia's ability to tap such institutions for capital to help rebuild its economy.

Bosnian Croat general Tihomir Blaskic, one of five others originally indicted with Aleksovski for war crimes committed in the Lasva Valley, handed himself over to the court in April last year. His trial has not yet started.
Nine other men have subsequently been charged with massacres and atrocities against Moslem civilians in the area. None have yet been apprehended.

Bosnian Moslems and Croats in the area fought side by side against separatist Serb forces when civil war first broke out in 1992, but the alliance collapsed in 1993 as they turned their weapons on each other in a bitter territorial struggle.
Both sides swapped accusations of gruesome massacres as villages were torched and people driven from their homes.
The tribunal says the Lasva Valley was ethnically cleansed by Croatian Defence Council (HVO) forces, with hundreds of civilians killed during the razing of Moslem villages.
"The pattern of attack was the same across the area. The villages were first shelled with an assortment of weaponry including mortars, rockets and anti-aircraft guns," it said.

"Groups of HVO soldiers then went from house to house killing and wounding Moslem civilians and finally burning houses barns and livestock. After the attacks subsided large numbers of civilians were detained."
The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia has so far indicted 75 war crimes suspects in the former Yugoslavia, but has only eight in its custody.
